name: Table Stakes
tagline: Futarchy for the kitchen table: vote on what better means, bet chores on what each option will do, and make the doubter own the outcome.
summary: Table Stakes brings futarchy to groups of three to thirty. Each quarter the group votes on two to four metrics, each paired with a lagging guard and filled from Stripe, PostHog, Plaid and the shared calendar, with a binary 'better or worse?' pulse capped at a third of the score. Big decisions go to sealed forecast rounds per branch, scored by the log rule and pooled by mean log-odds, and the best-forecast branch wins unless it breaks a hard constraint. The member who priced the winning branch lowest becomes its steward, earning a bonus for beating the other members' pooled forecast, or the group's base rate in groups too small for that. Teams stake points and households stake chore-hours, with a quarterly jubilee and no negative balances for minors, while a ledger tracks calibration by member and domain and a running commitment premium.
core_loop: Vote on metrics each quarter -> anyone proposes a decision with branches and a horizon -> members submit sealed forecasts per branch -> the best-pooled branch is chosen -> the lowest forecaster becomes steward -> weekly practice questions build calibration between decisions -> at the horizon the branch settles against measured metrics, log scores move points or chore-hours, the steward is paid for beating the benchmark, and the commitment premium (outcome minus forecast) is logged -> the quarterly jubilee clears balances.
why_now: MetaDAO showed conditional markets can run but saw revenue fall about 70% and pivoted, and the trends brief flags small-group futarchy as largely unbuilt. Kalshi and Polymarket volume and surging parlays have made conditional bets a mass-market idea, while metric APIs (Stripe, PostHog, Plaid) make passive, non-self-reported settlement cheap for small groups.
mvp: 90 days. Weeks 1-4: a Slack bot for 10 startups with sealed forecast rounds, log scoring, and Stripe and PostHog metric connectors. Weeks 5-8: the steward mechanic, weekly practice questions, and a WhatsApp beta for 30 households paying in chore-hours with a binary pulse. Weeks 9-12: measure repeat decisions, calibration and reported conflict. Kill metrics: under half of teams post a second decision within 30 days, or families report more conflict.
stack: Slack Bolt app and WhatsApp Business API bot; Stripe, PostHog, Plaid and Google Calendar connectors; a scoring engine for log scoring, mean log-odds pooling, base-rate benchmarks and binary robust Bayesian Truth Serum; Postgres.
business_model: Teams pay about $3 per seat per month, priced like Geekbot; households get a free tier, since household apps monetize poorly. Points are never convertible to money or bonuses, avoiding gambling and payroll questions.
risks: Groups make too few big decisions to form a habit once novelty fades
Traders can move the outcome; mitigated by stewardship, passive metrics and capping the self-reported pulse
Chore debt as a tool of coercive control; mitigated by the quarterly jubilee, no negative balances for minors and one-tap dissolution
Goodhart effects such as pulling MRR forward; mitigated by pairing each metric with a lagging guard
Information asymmetry: whoever holds the bank login or the data may dominate forecasts
Peer-prediction scoring breaks down if a family coordinates its pulse reports
Relationship harm when 'the app decided' replaces conversation
moonshot: A map of which decisions are forecastable. Ten years of commitment premiums across a million teams and households show which decisions are settled by foresight and which by someone deciding to win them. Co-ops, school boards and municipal budgets then send forecastable choices to markets and will-driven ones to stewards, and futarchy grows from the kitchen up rather than from the nation-state down.
best_line: The member who priced the winning branch lowest becomes its steward: 'disagree and commit', with a price on it.
